study.title: Psalm 98 The Lord reigns with salvation, justice and universal joy
study.overview: Psalm 98 calls the people of God to sing a new song because the Lord accomplished wonders, showed his salvation and revealed his righteousness to the nations. The psalm moves from the celebration of redemption already manifested for the convocation of all the earth, of the whole creation and, finally, of all peoples, to recognize the King who comes to judge with righteousness. The emphasis is not only on the deliverance of Israel, but on the public disclosure of God's righteous and faithful government over the whole world.

outline.title: The New Song of Salvation Revealed
outline.explanation: The first verses summon the worship because the LORD did wonders, overcame and made known his salvation. His righteousness appears before the nations, and his mercy and faithfulness toward Israel are remembered as the basis of this celebration.

outline.title: The whole earth is called to exult
outline.explanation: The proper response to God's saving action is a broad, cheerful and public praise. The text brings together the whole earth, with instruments and voice, to acclaim the Lord with enthusiasm and reverence.

outline.title: Creation participates in the hope of fair judgment
outline.explanation: The sea, the rivers, and the mountains are personified as rejoicing before the coming of the LORD. The final motive is his judgment to come: he will rule the world and the peoples with justice and righteousness.

study.context: The notes describe this psalm as a song about the reign of the LORD, with strong connection to the expectation of the Messianic government and the inclusion of nations. There is no basis for notes to set authorship or date for sure. The text is also presented as similar to Psalm 96, with the same focus on the coming of the King and the manifestation of his righteousness.
study.theology: The psalm unites salvation, justice and divine royalty. God not only redeems; he makes his salvation publicly known and shows that his government is correct. The remembrance of his goodness and faithfulness indicates that redemption is born of the character of God and the fulfillment of his promises. At the same time, judgment is not seen as an arbitrary threat, but as the consummation of his righteous reign over all the earth. In the evangelical reading of the notes, this points to the full fulfillment of the Messiah's government, in which salvation extends beyond Israel and reaches the nations.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm celebrates the kingship of the Lord and anticipates a world kingdom of righteousness, which is why the whole earth must worship him and rejoice at his coming.
The "new song" is that of the redeeming love of Christ, something that produces a new song in hearts transformed by grace.
The final verses present creation as a poetic figure who participates in joy before the coming of the righteous judge.

questions: How does God's knowing his salvation changes the way I love it today?
My worship expresses only personal gratitude or does it also recognize God's reign over all nations and peoples?
How is the certainty that God will judge the world with righteousness should shape my hope and attitudes in the face of the injustices present?
study.practice: Separate a moment to make Psalm 98 a prayer sung or read aloud, highlighting the verbs of the text: singing, screaming for joy, touching, rejoicing and acclaiming. Then write a concrete answer: an area where you need to rely more on God's justice and a practical attitude of praise that you can demonstrate this week, especially in the face of people who do not yet recognize the Lord.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not allow the security to affirm the authorship, the historical occasion or a technical sense of old terms without risk of speculation. There are also different interpretative readings among commentators on the extent of the Messianic reference and the way in which creation participates in the psalm; these readings should be treated as interpretations, not as absolute certainties of the text.
